title: AI Media Generation — Images, Audio & Video

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll understand the four categories of AI media generation (images, voice/audio, music, video), know the current best-in-class and free tools for each, learn how to write prompts that produce useful image output, and understand the specific failure modes that still limit each category. You'll generate your first AI image and explore at least one other category.

## The Media Generation Landscape (2026)

While text AI gets most attention, AI media generation has undergone its own revolution. Work that previously required professional software, production budgets, and specialist skills now produces usable outputs in seconds from a text description.

| Category | Free options | Best-in-class (paid) | Best use cases |
|----------|-------------|---------------------|----------------|
| **Image generation** | Bing Image Creator (DALL-E 3), Ideogram, Gemini Flash Image | Midjourney, Flux Pro, Recraft | Illustrations, concept art, social visuals, marketing |
| **Text-to-speech** | ElevenLabs free tier | ElevenLabs, PlayAI | Voiceovers, narration, accessibility |
| **Transcription** | Whisper (open source, free), FreeTranscriptions.com | Otter.ai, Descript | Meeting notes, lecture transcription, interview processing |
| **Music generation** | Suno free tier | Suno, Udio, Google Lyria | Background music, jingles, demo tracks |
| **Video generation** | Runway free tier | Sora 2, Google Veo 3, Kling 2, Runway Gen-4 | Short clips, concept visualisation, animation |

**The pace of change:** This is the fastest-moving area in AI. What is cutting-edge today becomes a free tier feature in 6-12 months. The skill to develop is not memorising specific tools — it's knowing what category to look for and how to evaluate new tools when they emerge. The underlying logic (text prompt → generated media) stays constant even as specific tools change.

## Image Generation — The Most Mature Category

AI image generation is the most developed and accessible media category. You describe an image in text and the model generates it. The quality gap between free and paid tools has narrowed significantly — free tools are genuinely good for many use cases.

**How the major tools differ:**

| Tool | Strengths | Weaknesses | Cost |
|------|-----------|-----------|------|
| ChatGPT (GPT-5.5 image gen) | Highly accurate, integrated in ChatGPT, best free quality | Fewer artistic style controls | Free (ChatGPT free tier) |
| Gemini Flash Image | Google's new image generation and editing model; excellent for photo-real and product shots | Newer — fewer style presets than Midjourney | Free (Gemini) |
| Bing Image Creator (DALL-E 3) | Easy access via Edge/Bing, no account required | Slightly lower quality than GPT-5.5 | Free |
| Ideogram | Best-in-class text rendering in images | Slower than others | Free tier |
| Midjourney | Highest aesthetic quality, photorealism | Paid-only; web interface (Discord no longer required) | $10-60/month |
| Flux Pro | Exceptional photorealism, good for people | Less stylised output | Paid per image |
| Recraft | Best for brand/UI/design consistency | Less suited for artistic images | Paid |
| Stable Diffusion | Fully local, completely free | Technical setup required | Free (local) |

**For most beginners:** ChatGPT's built-in image generation (available on the free tier with GPT-5.5) is now the recommended starting point — it's integrated into the same chat interface, requires no extra setup, and produces high-quality results. Gemini Flash Image and Bing Image Creator are solid free alternatives. Bing Image Creator requires no account in Microsoft Edge and handles most non-professional use cases well.

## Writing Image Prompts That Work

Image prompting is different from text prompting. The structure is more descriptive and visual, less instructional.

**The anatomy of an effective image prompt:**

```
[Subject] + [Action/Setting] + [Lighting/Atmosphere] + [Style/Medium] + [Technical details]
```

**Example — weak prompt:**
```
A coffee shop
```
→ Gets a generic, flat image with no character

**Example — strong prompt:**
```
A cozy independent coffee shop on a rainy day, warm amber interior lighting visible
through a fogged window, film photography style, shallow depth of field,
nostaligic mood, 35mm film grain
```
→ Gets a atmospheric, evocative image with the specific mood you wanted

**The most impactful elements to specify:**

**Subject and scene:**
- Be specific: "a Golden Retriever" not "a dog"
- Set the scene: "in a sun-drenched field of tall grass at late afternoon"
- Include action: "mid-jump, catching a frisbee"

**Lighting (huge impact on mood):**
- "golden hour light" — warm, long shadows
- "dramatic side lighting" — one strong directional source
- "soft diffused natural light" — even, gentle
- "neon-lit" — colourful, cyberpunk feel
- "candlelit" — warm, intimate, low light

**Style/medium:**
- "oil painting", "watercolor", "pencil sketch", "linocut print"
- "photorealistic", "digital art", "3D render", "flat design"
- "anime style", "Art Deco", "minimalist illustration"
- "film photography", "Polaroid", "35mm grain"

**Perspective/composition:**
- "bird's eye view", "worm's eye view", "wide establishing shot"
- "close-up portrait", "medium shot", "full body"
- "rule of thirds composition"

**What AI images still struggle with:**
- **Hands:** extra or missing fingers is still common — a known limitation across all tools
- **Readable text:** AI rarely renders legible words inside an image; use Ideogram if text matters
- **Exact faces:** depicting a specific real person accurately is unreliable (and often policy-restricted)
- **Complex scenes with many characters:** crowded scenes often have blending/proportion issues

## Text-to-Speech — Realistic AI Voice

**ElevenLabs** is the industry leader. You paste text, choose from hundreds of voices, and get natural-sounding speech — with proper intonation, natural pauses, and realistic breathing.

**Use cases that are production-ready today:**
- Voiceovers for YouTube videos without a recording setup
- Internal training videos with consistent narration
- Accessibility: audio versions of written content
- Podcast intros or transitions
- Demos and prototypes

**ElevenLabs free tier:** ~10,000 characters/month. Enough to narrate about 1,500 words — a short article or several shorter pieces.

**Voice cloning:** ElevenLabs and other tools can clone a voice from a short audio sample (about 1 minute). This creates legal and ethical obligations — cloning a voice without consent is problematic, and some jurisdictions are beginning to regulate it.

**Transcription (speech-to-text):**
The reverse capability — Whisper (OpenAI, free, open-source) transcribes audio with impressive accuracy across many languages. Practical workflow:
1. Record a meeting or lecture
2. Upload to a Whisper-powered service (many free web tools)
3. Paste the transcript into Claude → meeting summary + action items

This workflow replaces hours of manual note-taking.

## Music Generation and Video Generation

**Music Generation — Suno and Udio**

Suno generates complete music tracks — with instruments, structure, and optional vocals — from a text description. Free tier provides ~10 songs/day.

**Effective Suno prompts:**
```
Upbeat acoustic folk, 120 BPM, morning coffee mood, guitar and light percussion,
no lyrics, suitable for background music in a video
```

Or with lyrics:
```
An indie pop song about learning new skills, hopeful and energetic, female vocals,
electric guitar, verse-chorus-verse structure
```

**Realistic use cases today:** Background music for videos, podcast intros, demo tracks, jingle prototypes. Not a replacement for professional music production — but for everything that previously required either expensive licensing or compromising on quality, it's transformative.

**Video Generation — The Frontier (2026)**

Video generation has improved dramatically and is the category to watch most closely:

- **Sora 2** (OpenAI): Longer clips (up to 20 seconds), photorealistic, available in ChatGPT Pro
- **Google Veo 3**: Google's 2026 video generation model — powers NotebookLM's Cinematic Video Overviews; also available via Google Vertex AI and AI Studio. Strong at realistic motion and cinematic quality
- **Kling 2** (Kuaishou): Strong motion consistency, good for realistic human movement
- **Runway Gen-4**: Best for artistic and stylised content; free tier available

**Current realistic capabilities:**
- Short clips (5-20 seconds) of atmospheric or abstract content
- Animating a still image (make a photo come to life subtly)
- Visual concept exploration before committing to real production
- B-roll footage for video projects

**Still developing:** Longer narrative video, consistent characters across clips, complex human action, accurate dialogue synchronisation. Video generation is improving faster than any other AI category — what's a demo today becomes a production feature within months.

**Ethical and legal considerations for media generation:**
- **Deepfakes and consent:** Using AI to create realistic images or video of real people without their consent is illegal in many jurisdictions and always ethically problematic
- **Voice cloning:** Cloning someone's voice without consent may violate laws around impersonation, fraud, and personality rights
- **Copyright in training data:** Most image generation models were trained on copyrighted images. The legal status of AI-generated output's copyright is still being litigated
- **Transparency:** When using AI-generated media professionally, consider disclosing that AI was involved — some platforms and publishers now require this

These aren't reasons to avoid media generation tools entirely — they're reasons to be thoughtful about how you use them.

sections.title: Media Generation First Contact
sections.content:
This workshop is about first contact — experiencing what each category feels like. You're not mastering any tool, just building an intuition for what's possible.

**Part 1 — Required: Generate Your First AI Image**

Go to [Bing Image Creator](https://bing.com/images/create) — free, no account needed in Edge.

First, try this structured prompt:
```
A friendly robot reading a book in a cosy library, warm amber evening light,
watercolor illustration style, soft and detailed, books on shelves in background
```

Look at the four generated variations. Examine them carefully:
- Which one is your favourite and why?
- Check the hands — how many fingers?
- What did the AI get wrong or strange?

Now try **your own prompt** based on the prompt structure from this lesson:
```
[Subject] + [Setting/action] + [lighting description] + [style/medium]
```

Try 2-3 variations, adjusting the prompt based on what you didn't like in the first result.

**Part 2 — Choose one more category to explore**

Pick one of these:

**Music — Suno:**
- Go to [suno.com](https://suno.com) (free account or no account needed to explore)
- Click Create, describe a genre + mood + tempo + whether you want vocals
- Listen to what it generates

**Transcription — Upload an audio clip:**
- Go to [freeconvert.com/audio-to-text](https://www.freeconvert.com/audio-to-text) or any free Whisper-powered tool
- Record yourself speaking for 1 minute (Voice Recorder app in Windows)
- Upload and transcribe. See how accurate it is.

**Voice — ElevenLabs:**
- Go to [elevenlabs.io](https://elevenlabs.io) and create a free account
- Click Text to Speech
- Paste 2-3 sentences of text, choose a voice, click Generate
- Listen. Does it sound human?

**Write down after your exploration:**
- Which category surprised you most with its quality?
- What would you actually use one of these tools for in your real work?
- What are the limitations that would prevent professional use right now?

sections.question: You need text to appear legibly inside an AI-generated image — for example, a social media post with a quote printed on it. Which tool should you prioritise for this specific requirement?
options: Midjourney — it produces the highest quality images overall
Bing Image Creator — it's free and widely available
Ideogram — it's specifically designed for accurate text rendering within images
Stable Diffusion — as an open-source tool it gives more control
sections.explanation: Text rendering inside AI images is a known weakness across most image generation tools — they frequently produce garbled, misspelled, or illegible text. Ideogram was specifically built to solve this problem and consistently outperforms other tools at rendering legible text within generated images. This is the one scenario where 'which tool generates generally better images' is less important than 'which tool handles this specific requirement.'

sections.title: Workshop A — Prompt Refinement Drill
sections.content:
Practise the core skill: turning a vague image idea into a specific, structured prompt that produces the result you actually want. This builds the muscle memory for effective image prompting.

1. Go to [Bing Image Creator](https://bing.com/images/create) and open a second browser tab with Ideogram at [ideogram.ai](https://ideogram.ai).

2. Start with this deliberately vague prompt and generate it in Bing: **"A business meeting"**. Look at the result — note what assumptions the AI made about location, people, mood, and era.

3. Now expand the same idea using the full prompt anatomy: subject + setting + lighting + style + technical detail. Write your expanded version before generating. Example structure: *"Four diverse professionals in a modern glass-walled conference room, natural morning light through floor-to-ceiling windows, relaxed collaborative atmosphere, professional documentary photography style, wide angle shot"*.

4. Generate your expanded prompt. Compare the two results side by side. What specific changes in the prompt drove which changes in the output?

5. Now switch to Ideogram. Generate an image that must include a readable word or phrase — for example: *"A motivational poster with the bold text 'KEEP GOING' over a mountain sunrise, clean modern design, vibrant orange and blue, minimalist style"*. Check: is the text actually legible?

6. Go back to Bing Image Creator and generate the same text-heavy prompt. Compare the text legibility between the two tools.

7. AI-check step: Open Claude.ai and paste one of the images you generated (use the image upload button). Ask: *"Describe exactly what you see in this image. What looks unnatural, wrong, or strange?"* Note what the AI catches that you might have missed.

8. Reflection: Write one sentence in your notes describing what single prompt element made the biggest difference to image quality in your tests today.

sections.title: Workshop B — Create a Real Social Media Asset
sections.content:
You will produce a complete, usable social media image with a clear purpose — something you could actually post or use in your work.

1. **Choose your use case.** Pick one of these or define your own:
   - A motivational quote image for LinkedIn (must have readable text)
   - A header image for a blog post or newsletter article you're writing
   - A visual for a presentation slide covering a topic in your work
   - A profile or team photo stand-in (professional, atmospheric — no real people)

2. **Write a brief first.** Before prompting anything, write 3-5 sentences describing: what the image is for, who will see it, what mood or feeling it should convey, and what visual elements are essential vs. optional.

3. **Draft your first prompt** using the full anatomy: subject + action/setting + lighting + style/medium + technical details. Write it in your notes — not directly into the tool.

4. **Choose the right tool for the job:** If your image needs readable text, use Ideogram. If it's a photorealistic scene, use Bing Image Creator. If you need a highly designed or branded look, try both and compare.

5. **Generate your first version.** Screenshot or download the result.

6. **Identify 2 specific things to improve.** Be precise: not "it looks wrong" but "the lighting is too harsh" or "the font in the image is not legible" or "the people in the background look distorted."

7. **Revise your prompt** to address those two problems. Add or change only what targets those specific issues. Generate again.

8. **Compare versions 1 and 2.** Which prompt changes had the most impact? Generate a third version if needed.

9. **Download your best result.** Name the file with the prompt keywords so you can remember what worked.

10. **AI REVIEW step:** Open Claude.ai. Upload your final image. Paste this prompt: *"Don't validate this image — find 3 specific problems or gaps that would make it less effective as a professional social media asset. Be direct."* Read the feedback. Fix at least one issue by revising your image prompt and regenerating.

11. **Keep the final result.** You now have a real AI-generated asset and a tested prompt formula that works for this use case. Save both in a folder called `ai-media-assets`.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI Review of an Existing Visual
sections.content:
Take a visual from your real work — a presentation slide, a document header, a social media post, a product photo — and run adversarial AI review on it. This finds problems you've become blind to through familiarity.

1. Find a visual asset from your real work. This could be:
   - A slide from a presentation you've given or are preparing
   - A banner or header image from your company website or LinkedIn
   - A photo or image used in a recent document or report
   - Any image you created or chose for a professional purpose

2. If it's a slide or document, take a screenshot. If it's a web image, right-click and save it.

3. Open Claude.ai. Upload the image. Send this prompt: *"You are a professional visual communication consultant. Look at this image critically — don't be polite. List 3 specific problems with this image from a professional communication standpoint: what is unclear, visually weak, inconsistent, or likely to misfire with its intended audience? For each problem, suggest one concrete fix."*

4. Read all three critiques. For each one, decide: Is this feedback valid? Would fixing it make the image more effective?

5. Pick the one critique you most agree with. Ask Claude: *"How would I recreate this image using AI image generation to fix that specific problem? Give me a detailed prompt I could use in Bing Image Creator or Ideogram."*

6. Generate the improved version using the prompt Claude suggests. Compare the AI-improved version with your original.

7. In your notes: What did the adversarial review catch that you wouldn't have noticed on your own? Is the AI-generated alternative actually better, or did the original have qualities the AI version lacks?

sections.title: Workshop D — Media Generation Applied to Your Work
sections.content:
Apply media generation to a real, current need in your work. This is not a practice exercise — the output you create here should be something you actually use or seriously consider using.

1. **Identify a real need.** Think about work tasks coming up in the next 2 weeks where a visual, audio, or music element would help. Examples:
   - A presentation that needs better slide visuals
   - A training document or manual that would benefit from illustrations
   - A video project that needs background music or a voiceover
   - A social channel that needs a consistent visual style for posts
   - An internal newsletter that could use a header image each issue

2. **Pick the right category of media for your need:** image, voice/narration, music, or short video clip. Review the media landscape table from this lesson to choose the best tool.

3. **For images:** Write a prompt using the full structure. Generate 3-4 variations and select the best. Download it in the highest quality available.

4. **For voice/narration:** Go to ElevenLabs free tier. Write the script for a voiceover you actually need — a 30-60 second narration for a video, a podcast intro, or a short explainer. Choose a voice that matches your brand or context. Generate and download the audio file.

5. **For music:** Go to Suno. Write a prompt specifying genre, mood, tempo, instruments, and whether you want vocals. Generate 2-3 variations. Download the one that fits your context best.

6. **Assess fit for real use.** Ask yourself honestly: Would you actually use this output in a professional context as-is? What would it take to get it to that standard? (More iteration? A different tool? Minor editing in another app?)

7. **Document what worked.** Save the prompt that produced the best result. Note what you'd do differently on the next attempt. This is your growing library of prompts that work for your specific context.

sections.question: You want to create a short background music track for a 3-minute product demo video. You need something upbeat, professional, and royalty-free. Which approach gives you the fastest path to a usable result?
options: Hire a freelance musician on a platform like Fiverr — AI music is not professional quality yet
Use Suno's free tier with a detailed prompt specifying genre, mood, tempo, and 'no vocals, suitable for corporate video background'
Download free music from YouTube's Audio Library and use it without modification
Use the default background music in your video editing software
sections.explanation: Suno generates complete, original music tracks from text descriptions in seconds, and the free tier provides enough daily generations to iterate until you get something that fits. Specifying 'no vocals' and 'corporate video background' helps it produce clean, unobtrusive tracks. The output is original — no licensing concerns. Fiverr (A) is slower and costs money. YouTube Audio Library (C) has licence restrictions for commercial use. Default software music (D) is generic and often recognisable to viewers.

sections.question: You generate an AI image for a presentation, but the hands of the person in the image look wrong — too many fingers, strange proportions. What is the best immediate fix?
options: Accept the limitation — all AI images have hand problems and there is no workaround
Switch to a completely different image generation tool and start over
Add the phrase 'perfect anatomical hands, five fingers' to your prompt, or adjust the composition so hands are not the focal point
Use Photoshop to manually repaint the hands after downloading the image
sections.explanation: Prompting more explicitly for correct hands (e.g. 'perfect five-fingered hands, anatomically correct') sometimes improves results, but the most reliable quick fix is adjusting the composition: crop tighter to the face, use a pose where hands are partially hidden, or choose a wider shot where hands are small. Switching tools entirely (B) wastes time — hand issues exist across all tools. Photoshop (D) works but is slow and requires skill. Accepting it (A) is only appropriate when hands are not visible in the image.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 2-7.** You now have a complete map of the AI media generation landscape — image, voice, transcription, music, and video — with the practical knowledge of when free tools are sufficient, what current limitations to watch for, and how to write image prompts that get the result you want.
